title: Examination of the Self and Entities

slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter eighteen: the examination of the self and entities.

slides.heading: What is this 'I'?
points: Nothing feels more certain than 'I'
Yet when we try to say what it is, it slips away
The body? The mind? Something that has them?
slides.say: Nothing feels more certain than I. I am the one listening to these words, the one who was a child in an old photograph, the one who will wake up tomorrow. Yet when we try to say what this I is, it slips away. Is it the body? The mind? Something that has them? This chapter asks the question directly, and from the answer draws out the whole path: how suffering is kept going, how it stops, and what the Buddha meant when he spoke of self and of no-self.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: One of the shortest chapters, and most important
Gathers the search for the person in chapters 9 and 10
Contains verse 18.10, on dependence
slides.say: It is one of the shortest chapters and one of the most important. It gathers the search for the person in chapters nine and ten, completes the account of bondage in chapter sixteen and of karma in chapter seventeen, and contains the verse on dependence, eighteen point ten, that the owner's books return to again and again.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: The self and the aggregates
points: A person: five aggregates
Body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness
Is the self the same as them, or other?
slides.say: Now the explanation. Buddhism describes a person as five aggregates: body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. Verse eighteen point one asks how the self relates to them. There are two basic options, and both fail.

slides.heading: Same or other: both fail
slides.say: Suppose the self is the aggregates. Then it would arise and pass away as they do. Feelings change from moment to moment; perceptions come and go; the body is replaced cell by cell. A self that simply was these would be a new self every moment, and there would be as many selves as there are aggregates. That is not what I is taken to mean: the one who remembers, who lasts, who owns the feelings. Suppose instead the self is other than the aggregates. Then it would not have their marks. It would not be bodily, would not feel, perceive, intend or know. What would be left to call I? Every time we look for the self, we meet a sensation, a thought, a perception: an aggregate. A self different from all of them has never been met. Identity collapses the self into passing events; difference leaves a self with no marks at all. There is no third way for it to stand.

slides.heading: The mere I
points: Every other option rests on same or other
What is left is not 'no person'
Tsongkhapa's mere I: designated, never found
slides.say: The fuller searches of chapters nine and ten, and Chandrakirti's sevenfold analysis of the chariot, add the remaining options: the self inside the aggregates, the aggregates inside the self, the self owning them, the self as their collection or their shape. All depend on the self being either the same as the aggregates or different from them, so all fall with verse eighteen point one. What is left is not no person. Tsongkhapa calls it the mere I: the person designated in dependence on the aggregates, identical with none of them and found nowhere apart from them, yet fully able to remember, act, keep promises and change.

slides.heading: Not even an egoless one
points: 18.2: no self, so nothing truly 'mine'
18.3: but no 'egoless one' is found either
Liberation is not a refined, selfless self
slides.say: Verse eighteen point two draws the first consequence. If there is no self to own things, there is nothing that is truly mine. When the sense of self and the sense of ownership come to rest, one is free of I and free of mine. This is the classic aim of Buddhist practice. Verse eighteen point three immediately blocks a subtle mistake. It would be easy to picture the result as a new kind of person: the egoless one, the one who has gone beyond self. Nagarjuna says that this person is not found either. Whoever sees someone free of I is still seeing a someone, and has not seen. Liberation does not produce a refined self that has the quality of selflessness. It is the end of looking for a self, including a selfless one.

slides.heading: How the round stops
slides.say: Verses eighteen point four and five trace the mechanism of suffering backward, and show where it can be cut. When I and mine are used up, toward outer things and inner experience alike, grasping stops; and without grasping, no further birth is taken up. Verse five goes one level deeper. Liberation is the ending of action and afflictions. Action and afflictions arise from conceptual construction: the mind building up pleasant, unpleasant, mine, theirs, I am wronged. And conceptual construction arises from elaboration: the spinning-out of things as existing from their own side, ready to be named and reacted to. Elaboration, finally, stops in emptiness. The root is not a substance that must be destroyed, but a way of construing. When that construal stops, there is nothing for concepts, afflictions and actions to grow from.

slides.heading: In emptiness, or by emptiness
points: Chandrakirti: elaboration stops 'in emptiness'
Like darkness when a lamp is lit
Some modern scholars: 'by emptiness'
slides.say: Commentators read the last line in two ways. Chandrakirti reads in emptiness: elaboration stops when emptiness is realised, as darkness stops when a lamp is lit. Some modern scholars read by emptiness. The difference is small in practice. Either way, emptiness is not a new object that replaces the old ones. It is the seeing that the objects of elaboration were never there as elaborated.

slides.heading: Self, no-self, and neither
points: 18.6: the buddhas taught a self, no-self, and neither
A self, for those who deny that deeds have fruit
No-self, for those attached to a lasting self
slides.say: Verse eighteen point six can be surprising. The buddhas taught a self; they taught no-self; and they taught neither self nor no-self. How can all three be the teaching? Chandrakirti explains it as skilful teaching. To someone who thinks death is the end and actions have no consequences, the Buddha speaks of a self that experiences the fruit of its deeds. To someone attached to a lasting self, he teaches no-self. And to those ready for it, he teaches that neither a self nor a no-self is found as a thing, since no-self too is only a designation, not a new fact standing in the self's place.

slides.heading: The graded teaching
slides.say: Verse eighteen point eight gives the same graded pattern for reality as a whole. Everything is real is said to those who must first trust ordinary experience and its causes. Nothing is real is said to loosen grasping at things. Both joins the two: real conventionally, not real ultimately. Neither is for those who no longer need either label. Chandrakirti reads the four as steps for students at different stages, not as four claims to be believed at once. Each statement answers a particular grasping. None of them is a final description of a world standing on its own.

slides.heading: Where words stop
points: 18.7: where elaboration stops, so do words
The true nature: unarisen, unceasing
Like nirvana; not a realm beyond the world
slides.say: Verse eighteen point seven says why no single statement can be final. Where elaboration stops, what words can name and what thought can range over have stopped too. The true nature of things, unarisen and unceasing, is like nirvana. This is not a mystical realm beyond the world. It is what the homage of chapter one already said: dependent arising itself is without arising and ceasing.

slides.heading: The mark of reality
points: Seen for oneself, not known from another
At peace; not elaborated; free of construction
Without plurality: described by what is absent
slides.say: Verse eighteen point nine gives five marks of reality. It is not known by depending on someone else's description; it must be seen for oneself. Chandrakirti's example: someone with an eye disease sees hairs floating in the air. Being told that there are no hairs does not let them see their absence; but once the eye is cured, they see it for themselves. Reality is peaceful. It is not elaborated by elaborations. It is free of conceptual construction. And it is without plurality. The marks are mostly negative, and even at peace means that something has been stilled. Reality is described by what is absent from it: the overlay of elaboration. Nagarjuna does not install a positive absolute behind appearances. He removes what was added, and leaves appearances to be met without it.

slides.heading: Neither the same nor different
slides.say: Verse eighteen point ten is the most quoted line in this chapter, and perhaps in the owner's books. Whatever comes to be in dependence on something is not that very thing, and not other than it either. So it is neither cut off nor permanent. Take a rice seed and the rice plant that grows from it. The plant is not the seed: the seed is gone, and the plant has leaves and roots the seed never had. If they were the same, nothing would have grown. But the plant is not wholly other than the seed either: rice seed gives rice, never barley. If they were completely different, any seed could give any plant. Because they are not the same, the seed is not permanent. Because they are not different, the plant is not cut off from what went before. Sameness and difference both need two things with edges of their own to be compared. What arises in dependence has no such edges, so it escapes both.

slides.heading: The nectar of the teaching
points: Karma without a carrier; waking as the one who slept
18.11: not one, not many, not cut off, not permanent
18.12: the knowledge can arise without a teacher
slides.say: The verse applies everywhere. It explains how karma links a deed to its fruit without a carrier, how the person who wakes is the person who slept, and how continuity holds across a life without anything unchanged running through it. Verse eighteen point eleven calls this the nectar of the Buddha's teaching: not one, not many, not cut off, not permanent, four of the eight negations of the opening homage. And the last verse adds a quiet point. Even when no buddha has appeared and no disciples remain, the knowledge can arise in the solitary buddhas, who find it in seclusion. The truth taught here is not the private property of a tradition. It is how things are, open to anyone who looks closely enough.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: You still remember, answer to your name, keep promises
All of this belongs to the mere I
'I' and 'mine' stop being solid things to defend
slides.say: The chapter takes away a self that is found, and leaves the person fully in place. You still remember your childhood, answer to your name, keep your promises and live with the results of your choices. All of this belongs to the mere I, designated in dependence on body and mind. The practical result is not a blank. It is a loosening: I and mine stop being solid things to defend, and the grasping, anger and fear built on them lose their ground. Ethics, practice and teaching all keep their place.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapters 3, 9 and 14
The Logic of Dependency: the eight extremes; continuity
Anatta to Emptiness: Beyond the Extremes
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter three, on neither the same nor different, and the rice seed and sprout; chapter nine, on Tsongkhapa's mere I; and chapter fourteen, where the mere I keeps a promise for forty years. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, turns the eight extremes over and describes continuity without a carrier. In The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, Beyond the Extremes shows that no subject who was bound and is now free survives the analysis. There are also talks on YouTube: Core Logic 2, on identity and difference, and Carrierless Continuity. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter nineteen, the examination of time.
